explanation: At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, giving places inside the Arctic Circle the midnight sun. Around the December solstice they get polar night instead.

claims.text: North of the Arctic Circle, around the June solstice, the Sun stays above the horizon through the whole day and night.
Places just north of the Tropic of Cancer, the Equator or the Antarctic Circle still see the Sun set each day around the June solstice.
At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun.
Around the December solstice, places inside the Arctic Circle have polar night, with the Sun below the horizon all day.

Rival test: the Antarctic Circle is the natural confusion, but its midnight sun comes at the December solstice, and the stem says north of the line; the tropics and the Equator have sunsets every day. Against the key: atmospheric refraction lets the midnight sun appear a little south of the circle, which does not make any distractor right. evidence.restatement: North of the Arctic Circle the Sun stays up for at least one full day around the June solstice.
Near the Tropic of Cancer, the Equator and just north of the Antarctic Circle the Sun still sets daily in late June.
At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun.
Around the December solstice the Arctic has polar night, with the Sun below the horizon all day.

issues.note: c4 and the explanation's 'places inside the Arctic Circle get polar night': strictly, refraction lets places just inside the circle glimpse the Sun at noon on the December solstice. Textbook simplification, so a note only.

evidence.restatement: North of the Arctic Circle the Sun stays above the horizon all day and night around the June solstice.
Just north of the Tropic of Cancer, the Equator or the Antarctic Circle the Sun still rises and sets daily at the June solstice.
At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun.
Around the December solstice places inside the Arctic Circle have polar night.
